questions.qtext:
Two processes execute concurrently and attempt to implement mutual exclusion using two different locking mechanisms, namely LockA and LockB.

For LockA, a shared variable \( \texttt{turn} \) is used to decide whose turn it is. The variable is initially set to \( \texttt{turn} = 0 \).

For LockB, interrupts are disabled during the critical section. The system consists of a single processor unless stated otherwise.

The functions \( \texttt{disableInterrupts()} \) and \( \texttt{enableInterrupts()} \) respectively disable and enable interrupts on the given processor.

The code fragments executed by the processes are shown below. For simplicity, the code for Process \(P_0\) and Process \(P_1\) is written separately for LockA.

\[ \begin{array}{c|c|c} \text{LockA – Process } P_0 & \text{LockA – Process } P_1 & \text{LockB – Process } P_0 \text{ and } P_1 \\ \hline \\[-4pt] \begin{aligned}[t] &\text{/* turn initially = 0 */} \\ &\texttt{while (turn == 1);} \\ &\texttt{/* Critical Section */} \\ &\texttt{turn = 1;} \end{aligned} & \begin{aligned}[t] &\text{/* turn initially = 0 */} \\ &\texttt{while (turn == 0);} \\ &\texttt{/* Critical Section */} \\ &\texttt{turn = 0;} \end{aligned} & \begin{aligned}[t] &\text{/* Code for both } P_0 \text{ and } P_1 \text{ */} \\ &\texttt{disableInterrupts();} \\ &\texttt{/* Critical Section */} \\ &\texttt{enableInterrupts();} \end{aligned} \end{array} \]

Which of the following statements about the above locking mechanisms is/are TRUE?

options.text: LockA guarantees mutual exclusion and progress for both processes.
LockB guarantees mutual exclusion on both uniprocessors and multiprocessors.
LockA guarantees mutual exclusion but not progress.
LockB guarantees progress and mutual exclusion on a uniprocessor, but fails on multiprocessors and disables important interrupts.

questions.qtext:
Given two lists \( A \) and \( B \), each containing \( n \) integers, we want to find a one-to-one matching between elements of \( A \) and elements of \( B \) such that the total cost \[ \sum |a - b| \] over all matched pairs \( (a,b) \) is minimized.

For example, if \( A = \{4, -1, 8, 5\} \) and \( B = \{7, 9, 10, 3\} \), one possible matching is \( (-1,9), (4,7), (5,3), (8,10) \), which gives a total cost of \( |{-1}-9| + |4-7| + |5-3| + |8-10| = 17 \).


Which of the following algorithms correctly computes a minimum-cost matching between \( A \) and \( B \) in \( O(n \log n) \) time?

options.text: For each element of \( A \), greedily match it with the closest unused element of \( B \).
Sort both lists \( A \) and \( B \), and match the \( k \)-th smallest element of \( A \) with the \( k \)-th smallest element of \( B \).
Try all possible matchings between \( A \) and \( B \) and choose the one with minimum total cost.
Construct a complete bipartite graph between \( A \) and \( B \) with edge weights \( |a-b| \), and run Dijkstra’s algorithm.

Consider a source \(A\) that uses TCP to transfer a file of size \(8\,\text{KB}\) to destination \(B\). Each data packet carries a payload of \(1\,\text{KB}\). During the transfer, exactly two losses occur:

  • the $4$th data packet is lost, and
     
  • the acknowledgement of the $6$th data packet is lost.
     

Assume the following:

  • Retransmission timeout (RTO) \(= 4 \times \text{RTT}\)
     
  • Fast retransmission and fast recovery are triggered after receiving three duplicate acknowledgements
     
  • Connection setup time, processing time, and transmission time are ignored
     
  • Transfer time is measured from the instant the first data packet is transmitted by \(A\) to the instant the acknowledgement of the last data packet is received by \(A\)
     

How many RTTs are required to complete the entire file transfer?
